manuscripts.title: Donovan's Conjecture over Algebraically Closed Fields

candidates.label: Theorem 1.1
candidates.name: Donovan’s conjecture
candidates.heading: Theorem 1.1 (Donovan’s conjecture).
candidates.statement: Fix a prime p, an algebraically closed field K of character- istic p, and a positive integer M. As G ranges over finite groups and b over block idempotents of KG with defect groups of order at most M, only finitely many K-linear Morita equivalence classes of KGb occur. In particular, over this field K, Donovan’s conjecture holds for every finite p-group, including nonabelian groups.

candidates.label: Theorem 3.1
candidates.name: Fixed-root Cartan bound
candidates.heading: Theorem 3.1 (Fixed-root Cartan bound).
candidates.statement: Fix a finite collection R of root data and a finite collection of the usual pinned diagram automorphisms and exceptional diagram isogenies on these data. There is a constant C = C(R, p, M), also depending on this fixed collection of maps, with the following property. Let G be a connected reductive group over Fr, with root datum in R, and let F be a Steinberg endomorphism which, after an isomorphism of rational structures, has the form F = θ FrQ . Here Q is a power of r, FrQ is split Frobenius, and θ belongs to the specified finite collection; exceptional isogenies are allowed only in their prescribed defining characteristics. Put Γ = GF. For every subgroup Z ≤ Z(Γ) and every block b of k[Γ/Z] with defect groups of order at most M, all entries of the Cartan matrix of b are at most C.

candidates.label: Proposition 5.1
candidates.name: Labels and ordinary branching
candidates.heading: Proposition 5.1 (Labels and ordinary branching).
candidates.statement: The following conventions and formulas apply to the unipotent factors of the ordinary Jordan labels in the groups just specified. 1. For GLϵ n(q), where ϵ = 1 or −1, unipotent characters are indexed by partitions ν of n, and defp(χν) = ∏ h∈Hook(ν) (︁ (ϵq)h − 1 )︁ p . Here the p-part of a negative integer means the p-part of its absolute value. 2. In types B, C, D a symbol is a pair (A, B) of strictly increasing finite sets of nonnegative integers. Simultaneously replacing both rows A, B by {0} ∪ (A + 1), {0} ∪ (B + 1) does not change the symbol. The rows are unordered, subject to the usual two separate labels for equal rows in split type D of positive rank. If u = |A| + |B|, the rank is ∑ a∈A a + ∑ b∈B b − ⌊︃ (u − 1)2 4 ⌋︃ . 34 The difference |A| − |B| is odd in B, C, is 0 modulo 4 in split D, and is 2 modulo 4 in nonsplit D. We use one empty-group label in rank zero, and the toral convention for SO± 2 . A hook is a bead a and a smaller gap b in the same row; a cohook uses a gap in the other row. Their lengths are a − b > 0. For a packet with field parameter qi, its degree defect at the odd prime p is the product of (qh i − 1)p over hooks and (qc i + 1)p over cohooks. The inherited central torus contribution must also be included. For an original regular group this is its full connected center; for a residual factor R, it is the torus TR of Lemma 4.5. The product over packets, including a toral D1 packet, multiplied by |TF R|p, is the degree defect of the ordinary Jordan correspondent. Thus the toral packet is counted exactly once. 3. Lusztig induction from a single positive cycle torus of odd length d and a residual classical group adds d-hooks to symbols; a negative cycle adds d-cohooks. The coefficients have the usual leg signs, including the common extra minus sign for a cohook in type D. Each removal contributes absolute value one before the type-D identifications. The individual split labels are retained. Removing all cycles of the relevant length packs the runners and gives a core. Every unipotent label with that core occurs with nonzero coefficient in induction from the core and its cycle tori, with the appropriate residual orthogonal sign and, when necessary, the appropriate choice of split label. 4. Ordinary split Harish–Chandra restriction removes 1-hooks for GL, 2-hooks for GU with a GL1(q2) extraction, and same-row 1-hooks for symbols. On an ordinary Harish–Chandra series this is Young branching on partitions or bipartitions. In the unitary case the 2-core stays fixed; for symbols the row-length difference stays fixed up to exchange. The relative Weyl group is W(Bb), except for the zero-difference series in type D, where it is W(Db) and the branching keeps the two labels attached to equal bipartitions. At the first sign wall over a cuspidal symbol, the ratio of the two ordinary rank-one degrees is a power of qi, up to inversion. Over the unitary cuspidal staircase of size t(t + 1)/2 the ratio is q2t+1, up to inversion.

candidates.heading: Proposition 5.9 (Core block projections).
candidates.statement: In each remaining type-A unipotent target, and in each regular classical target with fixed p′-parameter s, the following holds. Each part is the intersection of that basic set with a union of blocks in Ep(HF, s). Distinct core collections cannot occur in the same block. manuscripts.title: Finite congruence lattices: characterization and undecidability

candidates.label: Theorem 1.1
candidates.heading: Theorem 1.1.
candidates.statement: The following statements hold. (i) A finite nonempty lattice is representable if and only if it satisfies the finite colored-graph criterion in Theorem 2.2. For each candidate graph size the criterion is decidable by a finite test. (ii) There is no deterministic Turing machine that, given the order table of a finite nonempty lattice, always halts and decides R(L). (iii) There is a nonrepresentable finite lattice L0 of minimum cardinality, specified by the finite formulas in Section 17. Every finite lattice of smaller cardinality is representable, and |L0| > 7. (iv) Given the order table of a finite nonempty lattice L, it is undecidable whether L ∼ = [H, G] for some finite group G and subgroup H ≤ G, where [H, G] is the full subgroup interval.

candidates.label: Theorem 2.2
candidates.name: Graph criterion
candidates.heading: Theorem 2.2 (Graph criterion).
candidates.statement: The lattice L is the full congruence lattice of a finite algebra if and only if there is an L-colored complete graph (A, d) satisfying all three conditions below. (i) If p ̸= q, then d(p, q) ̸= 0, and d(p, q) ≤ d(p, u) ∨ d(u, q) (p, q, u ∈ A). (ii) Whenever a ̸≤ b in L, there are vertices p, q with d(p, q) ≤ a and d(p, q) ̸≤ b. (iii) For every nonempty edge set S, vertices p, q satisfying d(p, q) ≤ aS lie in the same connected component of ΓS. 7 For each fixed |A|, these conditions involve only lattice inequalities, finite vertex labelings, and paths.

candidates.label: Corollary 2.3
candidates.name: Enumeration and bounds
candidates.heading: Corollary 2.3 (Enumeration and bounds).
candidates.statement: Representability is semidecidable. Moreover, a total algorithm deciding representability of finite lattice order tables exists if and only if there is a total computable function b : N>0 → N>0 such that every representable lattice L has a graph witness in Theorem 2.2 with at most b(|L|) vertices.

candidates.label: Proposition 3.2
candidates.heading: Proposition 3.2.
candidates.statement: With their usual subfield inclusion, the groups H = PGL2(F2) ≤ G = PGL2(F64) have subgroup interval [H, G] ∼ = L7.

candidates.label: Theorem 3.4
candidates.heading: Theorem 3.4.
candidates.statement: Every finite nonempty lattice of at most seven elements is representable.

candidates.label: Theorem 4.1
candidates.heading: Theorem 4.1.
candidates.statement: There are choices of the finite parameters in Definition 4.4 for which the resulting finite lattice is not the congruence lattice of any finite algebra.

candidates.label: Proposition 4.5
candidates.name: Geometry of the test lattice
candidates.heading: Proposition 4.5 (Geometry of the test lattice).
candidates.statement: The construction in Definition 4.4 gives a finite self-dual lattice L. It is graded of length n + 2, atomistic, coatomistic, and simple. Any two charts 13 intersect in a flat of each, of rank at most m, with the same affine structure on the intersection. Within one chart the primal join of two flats is their affine span if that span has dimension at most n. Attachment preserves all old meets and joins. In particular, flats in two distinct private charts attached at the same W, neither contained in W, have no common proper primal upper bound. There are at least three horizontal comparability components in the interior of L, each containing a chain of distinct comparable interior elements.

candidates.label: Proposition 4.6
candidates.name: Prepared reverse links
candidates.heading: Proposition 4.6 (Prepared reverse links).
candidates.statement: If X is a nonempty flat of rank at most m in a trunk chart, the reverse ideal with top X, denoted [0, X], is graded, atomistic, and coatomistic. Its strict interior has at least two horizontal comparability components, each containing comparable distinct elements. The following additional properties hold for L and for every such prepared link. (i) Every bottom interval of length two is a diamond Mb with b ≥ 3 atoms, where b − 1 ≥ 2 is not a prime power. (ii) In every interior component there is an element y two ranks below the interval’s top whose upper interval is a diamond with at least two middle elements. 14 In addition, L has the following separation property: (iii) For any atom u and any proper upper bound ω ≥ u, there is a rank-two element z ≥ u with z ̸≤ ω.

candidates.label: Proposition 4.8
candidates.heading: Proposition 4.8.
candidates.statement: If the test lattice L is representable by a finite algebra, it is isomorphic to an ordinary subgroup interval of a finite group.

candidates.label: Proposition 4.9
candidates.name: Normal supplements
candidates.heading: Proposition 4.9 (Normal supplements).
candidates.statement: Suppose [H, G] is isomorphic either to L or to a prepared reverse link. After quotienting by coreG(H), every nontrivial normal subgroup is supplemented by H. The quotient has a unique minimal normal subgroup M = Ss, with S nonabelian simple, and H acts transitively on its simple factors. Moreover CG(M) = 1 in the core quotient. In that quotient the subgroup interval identifies with [P, Ss ]H , P = H ∩ Ss , (4.4) the H-invariant subgroups in this range, by intersection with Ss; the inverse sends Y to HY .

candidates.label: Proposition 4.11
candidates.name: Cases for a prepared interval
candidates.heading: Proposition 4.11 (Cases for a prepared interval).
candidates.statement: Use the notation of Proposition 4.9, in the core quotient. Let Λ ≤ Aut(S) be the image of a coordinate stabilizer in H, and put I = Λ ∩ S, identifying S with its inner automorphisms. The following are the only possibilities. (i) c(P) = Ss. All labels are subdirect. If the interval represents the whole L, its opposite has an ordinary subgroup representation with top-group order at most |H| < |G|. (ii) P = c(P) ̸= 1. The interval is isomorphic to the ordinary almost simple interval [Λ, SΛ]. (iii) P = 1 and I = S. Every nonbottom label is subdirect, and the dual interval is the extension poset of Lemma 4.10 with one artificial top adjoined. In particular the cases P < c(P) < Ss, P = 1 with I = 1, and P = 1 with 1 < I < S are impossible.

candidates.label: Theorem 4.15
candidates.name: Ordinary almost simple starting interval
candidates.heading: Theorem 4.15 (Ordinary almost simple starting interval).
candidates.statement: If the test lattice L is representable, then either the whole L or a prepared reverse link with top an initial trunk point has an ordinary almost simple subgroup-interval representation. On the reverse side, there are at least D − 1 further generations of prepared stages starting at that top. This conclusion uses only the field condition and (4.1), independently of later choices of larger parameters.

candidates.label: Proposition 5.4
candidates.name: Finite schedule of simultaneous exclusions
candidates.heading: Proposition 5.4 (Finite schedule of simultaneous exclusions).
candidates.statement: Suppose that the local exclusions below prohibit their prescribed failed patterns with absolute case and chart-loss bounds. For a bounded path length, finitely many rounds then produce a flat of final increment r such that the subgroup label of every proper extension in it is contained in none of the prescribed proper full stabilizers relative to any high-type ancestor. The next local simple has the corresponding transitivity or full-spanning properties relative to all those ancestors.

candidates.label: Proposition 5.5
candidates.name: Order of the finite parameter choices
candidates.heading: Proposition 5.5 (Order of the finite parameter choices).
candidates.statement: The test-lattice parameters can be chosen in an order that meets all the pattern requirements and all the later path requirements. In particular the initial height-dependent pattern requirement does not create a circular dependence between m, n, N. Once the local group results are applied, these choices force either the bounded-type contradiction or a path longer than the protected-path bound.

candidates.label: Proposition 6.4
candidates.name: Linear subspaces, signed flags and idempotents
candidates.heading: Proposition 6.4 (Linear subspaces, signed flags and idempotents).
candidates.statement: In linear type, the initial round excludes stabilizers of proper nonzero subspaces when there are no anti-actions. In the presence of anti-actions it excludes signed flags 0 < I ≤ J < V and individual proper nontrivial idempotents. candidates.heading: Proposition 6.29 (Completion of tensor-system pruning).

candidates.name: The next classical-ancestor socle
candidates.heading: Theorem 6.30 (The next classical-ancestor socle).
candidates.statement: Let K be a tested descendant with a prepared interval, good for all the exclusions in this section, or containing the final good anchor. candidates.label: Theorem 8.2
candidates.name: Sufficiently general finite subgroups
candidates.heading: Theorem 8.2 (Sufficiently general finite subgroups).
candidates.statement: For the fixed finite list of simple adjoint types, there is a uniform degree bound d0 with the following property. If a finite subgroup Γ ≤ G(k), where k = Fp, is contained in no proper closed subset of equation complexity at most d0, then there is a Steinberg map Ψ such that (GΨ )′ ≤ Γ ≤ GΨ . Here the degree bound follows from the uniform constructible-family formulation of the sufficiently- general subgroup theorem of Larsen–Pink [25, Theorem 0.5 and Metadefinition 2.2]: the exceptional family has uniformly bounded defining equations in the fixed affine models.

There is a fixed trial increment t such that a prepared current parent with a remaining private-chart stage cannot have socle of one of these types, provided the residual interval length is sufficiently large. candidates.statement: Let B be as in Lemma 9.7, in the high classical ancestor with adjoint group Gi and ordinary Steinberg map Φi of height fi. candidates.heading: Corollary 9.10 (Equal natural modules force a fixing root).
candidates.statement: Suppose B < Si is a same-series high classical candidate of the same natural dimension as Si, and its projective action on Vi is its own natural module, allowing a Frobenius twist and, in type A, a diagram natural/dual twist. Then some prime root of Φi fixes B pointwise. Thus the absence of such fixing roots excludes this case.

candidates.label: Proposition 9.12
candidates.name: Selecting all ancestor protections
candidates.heading: Proposition 9.12 (Selecting all ancestor protections).
candidates.statement: Assume that the current same-characteristic classical run is already protected through its current node W. Fix an upper bound D on the number of path steps and a fixed number c of continuation colors. There is a finite extension rank r, depending only on D, c and earlier fixed requirements, such that from every suitably pruned private chart at a current high classical node one can select a next proper extension. If that extension continues the current same-characteristic run, it has both protections relative to every ancestor in that run, including the current node. Earlier structural exclusions are preserved.

candidates.label: Proposition 9.15
candidates.name: Composing the rational highest-weight actions
candidates.heading: Proposition 9.15 (Composing the rational highest-weight actions).
candidates.statement: Let i < j < l lie in one protected run, and suppose these three nodes have the same series A, B, C, or D. Use consistent natural realizations and simply connected covers of the actual nested simple subgroups. Write Gs = b Gj and J = b Gl. The lifted edge representations ij and jl have highest weights px λ, py η, where λ, η ̸= 0 are p-restricted. The latter representation induces an algebraic homomorphism J → (Gs)ad which lifts to J → Gs. The resulting rational composition of LGs (pxλ) is irreducible. Its highest weight µ is one nonzero p-digit times a power of p, and that digit has the shape, up to diagram, of the direct edge il.

candidates.label: Proposition 9.18

candidates.heading: Proposition 9.18 (No homogeneous type A configuration).

candidates.label: Theorem 9.21
candidates.name: Bound on protected high-type paths
candidates.heading: Theorem 9.21 (Bound on protected high-type paths).
candidates.statement: There is an absolute constant D0 such that a prepared path all of whose socles are of high alternating or high classical type, and whose consecutive same-characteristic classical runs are protected, has fewer than D0 nodes. This constant is independent of all chart dimensions, finite fields, and path-construction parameters.

candidates.label: Theorem 10.1
candidates.name: Reverse alternating exclusion
candidates.heading: Theorem 10.1 (Reverse alternating exclusion).
candidates.statement: For all sufficiently large integers v, the lattice Sub(Av)op has no exact realization as [P, Sb ]∆ , where S is nonabelian simple, ∆ acts by automorphisms transitively on the b simple factors, P is a ∆-invariant coordinate product, and either P ̸= 1 or b = 1.

candidates.label: Theorem 11.6
candidates.name: Forward marker theorem
candidates.heading: Theorem 11.6 (Forward marker theorem).
candidates.statement: For every nonnegative integer m, there are integers a(m) and t0(m) such that the following holds whenever |T| ≥ t0(m). Every exact forward realization FT = [P, Sb ]∆ with S nonabelian simple, ∆ transitive on the factors, and invariant coordinate product P ̸= 1 (or b = 1), has the following configuration in the ordinary site interval of Lemma 11.5. There is A ⊂ T with |A| ≤ a(m) such that KMA has an actual high-degree alternating simple normal subgroup BA ≤ S satisfying HBA = KMA , CKMA (BA) ≤ H, CKMA (BA) is soluble. In the almost simple quotient KMA /CKMA (BA), at least m distinct labels MA∪{i}, with fresh indices i ∈ T \ A, are full stabilizers of individual points in the natural alternating action. The constants a(m) and t0(m) are independent of S, b, ∆, P and the realization; the high-degree threshold is the fixed one used in the structural exclusions.

candidates.label: Proposition 11.16
candidates.name: Subset stabilizers produce points
candidates.heading: Proposition 11.16 (Subset stabilizers produce points).
candidates.statement: If a tested descendant is contained in a proper subset stabilizer, then, after the finite selections of Lemma 11.15, there are arbitrarily many distinct relative labels M{i} that are full stabilizers of individual natural points. In absolute notation these are MA∪{i}. Consequently, in the absence of the conclusion of Theorem 11.6, the required descendants and their bounded intersections are transitive.

candidates.label: Proposition 11.18
candidates.name: Exclusion of affine and Cartesian structures
candidates.heading: Proposition 11.18 (Exclusion of affine and Cartesian structures).
candidates.statement: After Lemma 11.17, the tested descendants are primitive. They cannot lie in full normalizers of elementary abelian regular groups or in proper Cartesian-system stabilizers.

candidates.label: Proposition 11.22
candidates.name: Maximality of an unbalanced ordered splitting
candidates.heading: Proposition 11.22 (Maximality of an unbalanced ordered splitting).
candidates.statement: Let V = W ⊕ U, with 0 < dim U < dim W, be a nondegenerate splitting in an isometry type, or an image–kernel splitting in linear type with anti-actions. Let M be a group of the corresponding classical actions containing the natural special group, and let K be the full ordered splitting stabilizer, equivalently the idempotent stabilizer for the ring action. Assume that K supplements the special group in M, that its collineations act semilinearly irreducibly on U, and that the supported special group on W is available, as is that on U when dim U is large. In the linear case assume also that K contains an anti-action fixing the projector, hence carrying its image–kernel data into the dual annihilator data. For sufficiently large dim W, the subgroup K is maximal in M.

candidates.label: Proposition 11.25
candidates.name: Exclusion of proper projectors
candidates.heading: Proposition 11.25 (Exclusion of proper projectors).
candidates.statement: Under the preceding classical rounds, the tested descendants cannot lie in any of the proper stabilizers considered in Lemma 11.23. The remaining descendants and the required bounded intersections therefore have irreducible anchors; in linear type their collineation parts are also irreducible.

candidates.label: Proposition 11.29
candidates.name: Exclusion of the remaining direct systems
candidates.heading: Proposition 11.29 (Exclusion of the remaining direct systems).
candidates.statement: After the preceding classical rounds, a homogeneous family of proper full direct-system stabilizers cannot occur at the tested descendants.

candidates.label: Proposition 11.32
candidates.name: Maximality of an unequal ordered tensor factor
candidates.heading: Proposition 11.32 (Maximality of an unequal ordered tensor factor).
candidates.statement: Let S be a high-rank classical simple group on V , and let an ordered proper matrix tensor factor give natural dimensions x < y, both sufficiently large. In isometry type assume that the factor is selfadjoint. In characteristic two assume that the bilateral factor forms are alternating, and in orthogonal type use the canonical tensor quadratic form. Exclude symplectic type in characteristic two. Then the full stabilizer in S of the ordered factor is maximal.

candidates.label: Proposition 12.1
candidates.name: Field and paired overgroups in the prepared configuration
candidates.heading: Proposition 12.1 (Field and paired overgroups in the prepared configuration).
candidates.statement: Use the transferred forms of Section 6. Let D ⊆ A be a field containing F, with [D : F] = n, where n is prime or a product of two distinct primes, and let m = v/n be sufficiently large. In an isometry type assume that D is selfadjoint; in orthogonal characteristic two assume the irreducible normalization already obtained in the preceding rounds. Omit symplectic characteristic two with nontrivial adjoint on D. Alternatively, in an isometry type other than symplectic characteristic two, let e, e∗ = 1 − e be exchanged complementary idempotents, with totally singular images when a quadratic form is present, and let m = v/2 be sufficiently large. Suppose that the collineation action of each overgroup under consideration is semilinearly irreducible, as ensured here by the previous-good axis. Every proper overgroup in M of the full field stabilizer preserves a nontrivial subfield algebra of D over F. Every proper overgroup of the full paired stabilizer preserves that pair. Consequently a prime-degree field stabilizer and an exchanged-pair stabilizer are maximal; for a compositum of two prime degrees its maximal overgroups can only be the stabilizers of its prime-degree subfields.

candidates.label: Proposition 12.3
candidates.name: Exclusion of two large ordered factors
candidates.heading: Proposition 12.3 (Exclusion of two large ordered factors).
candidates.statement: At the present forward-test stage, a homogeneous family of failures preserving proper ordered matrix tensor factorizations cannot have both factor degrees above the fixed large-degree threshold. In isometry types the factors are selfadjoint and have the normalized factor forms.

candidates.label: Proposition 12.6
candidates.name: Exclusion of fields, pairs, and nuisance planes
candidates.heading: Proposition 12.6 (Exclusion of fields, pairs, and nuisance planes).
candidates.statement: In the prepared forward-test configuration, the prime-field and exchanged-pair failures are impossible. The nuisance planes of Lemma 12.4 are therefore impossible as well, completing the ordered-factor exclusion.

candidates.label: Proposition 12.8
candidates.name: Exclusion of permuted tensor systems
candidates.heading: Proposition 12.8 (Exclusion of permuted tensor systems).
candidates.statement: After the preceding rounds, neither a full-algebra elementary abelian normalizer nor a nontrivial permuted tensor-system stabilizer can be a failure label in the forward test.

candidates.label: Proposition 12.9
candidates.name: Grounding at bounded omissions
candidates.heading: Proposition 12.9 (Grounding at bounded omissions).
candidates.statement: After the prescribed rounds, every tested descendant has an actual nested normal simple supplement with soluble centralizer in the base. Relative to a high classical ancestor it is absolutely irreducible and avoids all the excluded tensor structures. Relative to an alternating ancestor it is primitive and transitive unless the desired point configuration has already been obtained. Its simple type can be required to exceed any fixed bounded order or bounded-rank threshold. The same actual normal simplicity and full spanning apply to a label above a previous-good axis and below the ancestor when it has the indicated nonabelian part: either a contained perfect simple group as used here, or its own pure link satisfying the normal test. In the first case that perfect group lies in the resulting normal simple.

candidates.label: Proposition 12.19
candidates.name: Singleton tensor failures
candidates.heading: Proposition 12.19 (Singleton tensor failures).
candidates.statement: The singleton coatom witnesses in Lemma 12.11 cannot be prime tensor-coarsening stabilizers.

candidates.label: Proposition 12.20
candidates.name: Completion of the forward marker argument
candidates.heading: Proposition 12.20 (Completion of the forward marker argument).
candidates.statement: The forward marker assertion of Theorem 11.6 holds. In the prepared configuration, the assumption of no point success at all the prescribed bounded prefixes is impossible once the initial marker set is sufficiently large.

candidates.label: Proposition 13.6
candidates.name: From algebras to ordinary intervals
candidates.heading: Proposition 13.6 (From algebras to ordinary intervals).
candidates.statement: Every nilpotent join-preserving deflation of F̄ is zero. If some nontrivial image of F is the congruence lattice of a finite algebra of size m, there is an ordinary finite-group interval representing the dual of a nontrivial image of F, whose top group has order at most 60mm!. The full lattice F itself has a finite algebra representation.

candidates.label: Proposition 13.11
candidates.name: Normal endpoint property for weighted images
candidates.heading: Proposition 13.11 (Normal endpoint property for weighted images).
candidates.statement: For sufficiently large absolute cohort stock, every ordinary interval representing a nontrivial weighted image, in either orientation, satisfies (∗). Its base acts transitively on the simple factors of its monolith modulo the base core. The same assertion holds for the bounded axis deletions used here, provided the remaining stock is sufficient.

candidates.label: Proposition 13.13
candidates.name: Forward proper projections
candidates.heading: Proposition 13.13 (Forward proper projections).
candidates.statement: In a forward realization [P, W]H, suppose P > 1 and c(P) < W. Every cut coatom is a product label. If P < c(P), its closure label has empty footprint and lies below J∗.

candidates.label: Proposition 13.18
candidates.name: Reverse projections and the trivial-base cases
candidates.heading: Proposition 13.18 (Reverse projections and the trivial-base cases).
candidates.statement: In reverse orientation, if P > 1, then c(P) = W. If P = 1, every nonidentity actual label is subdirect and the site-action image Λ contains the inner automorphisms of S. In forward orientation with P = 1, either a marker axis filter gives product success, or the same subdirectness and inner-action conclusions hold.

candidates.label: Theorem 13.19
candidates.name: Product success with absolute stock
candidates.heading: Theorem 13.19 (Product success with absolute stock).
candidates.statement: There are absolute stock and marker-loss bounds with the following property. Any ordinary realization, in either orientation, of a nontrivial weighted image yields a forward realization of a nontrivial image of the weighted template with at most boundedly many markers deleted, in which product success holds. The stock bound is independent of all numerical unit sizes and of the number of cohorts. The simple group at a site has order at most the original top-group order. A larger prescribed fixed stock can be retained by increasing the initial absolute stock.

candidates.label: Proposition 13.23
candidates.name: Common alignment of all cuts
candidates.heading: Proposition 13.23 (Common alignment of all cuts).
candidates.statement: There is a single bijection from the formal units together with the foundation position to the Θ-orbits on Ω, under which every cut and every intersection of cuts is the corresponding stabilizer of unions of those orbits. Write uj > 0 for the size of the cell of unit j. The specified genuine point markers have size one.

candidates.label: Proposition 13.24
candidates.name: Equal totals and equal copies
candidates.heading: Proposition 13.24 (Equal totals and equal copies).
candidates.statement: Let D, E be disjoint bounded collections of nonfoundation units with equal formal total size, with ample spare markers outside them. If at least one of D, E contains more than one unit, then X j∈D uj = X j∈E uj. In a sufficiently numerous cohort, all copies have the same actual cell size. In particular, all surviving markers have size one.

candidates.label: Theorem 13.25
candidates.name: Reading a primary square
candidates.heading: Theorem 13.25 (Reading a primary square).
candidates.statement: For a primary square O and its full side reference R, let r = uR in the alignment of Proposition 13.23. If r is even and r ≥ 8, then uO = r2.

candidates.label: Theorem 13.26
candidates.name: Weighted realization and simultaneous numerical readings
candidates.heading: Theorem 13.26 (Weighted realization and simultaneous numerical readings).
candidates.statement: Fix any bounded support size for the comparisons and any desired fixed number of spare copies. There are absolute initial cohort-stock and marker-loss bounds, independent of the numerical unit sizes and the number of cohorts, with the following property. The bounds may depend on the fixed support and spare-copy requirements. An ordinary realization of a nontrivial weighted image, in either orientation and with top order M, gives a forward realization after at most that many marker deletions, with all cuts product in an actual alternating power. A single common cell alignment gives positive sizes uj ≤ M, equal on each cohort and one on all surviving markers. In this same alignment the equal-total reading of Proposition 13.24 and the square reading of Theorem 13.25 hold. If the input is a finite algebra of size m representing a nontrivial image, the same conclusion holds with M = 60mm!, for a possibly different nontrivial image of the original template. The full template itself is finitely representable.

candidates.label: Proposition 14.6
candidates.name: Rank-one overgroups
candidates.heading: Proposition 14.6 (Rank-one overgroups).
candidates.statement: There are computable functions of s that bound, for every rank-one control X of complexity at most s on a finite nonempty set I, (i) the number of transitive groups U with X ≤ U ≤ SI and the index [U : ⟨XU ⟩]; 150 (ii) the length of a generating list for U over X, chosen so that every generator g has a rank-one control of computably bounded complexity inside X ∩ gXg−1.

candidates.label: Proposition 14.7
candidates.name: Overgroups of controls with private squares
candidates.heading: Proposition 14.7 (Overgroups of controls with private squares).
candidates.statement: There are computable functions B(s), C(s) such that every control X with private squares of complexity at most s on a finite nonempty set I has at most B(s) transitive overgroups in SI, and every such overgroup U satisfies [U : ⟨XU ⟩] ≤ C(s). The functions can be taken nondecreasing and at least one.

candidates.label: Theorem 14.8
candidates.name: Uniform computable template bound
candidates.heading: Theorem 14.8 (Uniform computable template bound).
candidates.statement: There is a total computable nondecreasing function Φ : Z≥0 → Z≥1 such that every weighted template F = [SZ × Y, SZ⊔( S T)] 154 of Section 13, with at most t units, excluding the foundation Z from this count, and |Z| > | S T|, satisfies |F| ≤ Φ(t). The bound is independent of all full-unit sizes, square sides, auxiliary axis lengths, offset sizes, and the size of Z. No stock-size hypothesis is required for this counting assertion.

candidates.label: Theorem 15.3
candidates.name: Undecidability of finite representability
candidates.heading: Theorem 15.3 (Undecidability of finite representability).
candidates.statement: There is no algorithm which, given the tables of a finite lattice, decides whether it is isomorphic to the congruence lattice of a finite algebra. Equivalently, there is no total computable bound, in terms of lattice cardinality, for the minimum carrier size among all representable finite lattices.

candidates.label: Corollary 15.4
candidates.name: Undecidability of finite subgroup-interval recognition
candidates.heading: Corollary 15.4 (Undecidability of finite subgroup-interval recognition).
candidates.statement: There is no deterministic Turing machine which, given the order table of a finite nonempty lattice L, always halts and decides whether L ∼ = [H, G] for some finite group G and subgroup H ≤ G, where [H, G] consists of every subgroup K with H ≤ K ≤ G, ordered by inclusion. Equivalently, there is no total computable bound, in terms of lattice cardinality, on the least possible order of the top group G among lattices admitting such a realization.

candidates.label: Proposition 16.5
candidates.name: Quantitative genericity
candidates.heading: Proposition 16.5 (Quantitative genericity).
candidates.statement: Let x ≥ 109, and let G be adjoint simple of rank at most x over an algebraically closed field of characteristic p > 0. If a finite subgroup Γ ≤ G is not contained in any proper closed subset of affine ring format at most J1000(x), then there is a positive-height standard point map Ψ such that (GΨ )′ ≤ Γ ≤ GΨ . (16.4) Proper closed subsets in this hypothesis need not be irreducible.

candidates.label: Theorem 16.7
candidates.name: Size ceiling
candidates.heading: Theorem 16.7 (Size ceiling).
candidates.statement: The negative affine-chart construction has a choice of finite parameters for which its lattice L is nonrepresentable and |L| < M∗. In particular a nonrepresentable lattice exists among the tables of cardinality at most the ordinary computable integer M∗.

candidates.label: Theorem 17.9
candidates.name: Finite description of a minimum example
candidates.heading: Theorem 17.9 (Finite description of a minimum example).
candidates.statement: The bounded formulas (17.13)–(17.16), with the ordinary unevaluated Busy Beaver constant (17.1), specify the full finite order table of a nonrepresentable lattice L0 of minimum cardinality. Its cardinality is the integer a0 in (17.15), and 7 < a0 ≤ M∗. This is a finite order description and a proof of minimum cardinality; it does not supply a numerically evaluated value of that cardinality.

manuscripts.title: A negative solution to the finite lattice representation problem

candidates.label: Theorem 1.1
candidates.heading: Theorem 1.1.
candidates.statement: There exists a finite nonempty lattice L such that L ̸∼ = Con(A) for every finite nonempty algebra A of every finite signature.

candidates.label: Theorem 1.2
candidates.heading: Theorem 1.2.
candidates.statement: There exists a finite lattice that is not isomorphic to [D, G] for any subgroup D of any finite group G.

candidates.label: Corollary 2.4
candidates.name: Bottlenecks
candidates.heading: Corollary 2.4 (Bottlenecks).
candidates.statement: Let D < B ≤ Z, suppose that [D, B] is fenced, and suppose that B is comparable with every member of [D, Z]. If R ⊴ Z and R ≰ D, then B = D(R ∩ B). Consequently a soluble normal subgroup of Z is contained in D. If R, Q ⊴ Z and [R, Q] ≤ F ⊴ Z, F ≤ D, then at least one of R, Q is contained in D. These conclusions also hold with B = Z.

candidates.label: Proposition 2.6
candidates.name: Equal-type transport
candidates.heading: Proposition 2.6 (Equal-type transport).
candidates.statement: Let D < X < Y be labelled vertices. Then FY ≤ FX, and TX is isomorphic to a section of TY . Put EX = (X ∩ NY )/FY ≤ SY . The following conditions are equivalent: (i) TX ∼ = TY ; (ii) EX is subdirect in SY . When they hold, the quotient map induces an isomorphism EX ∼ − − → SX, NX = FX(X ∩ NY ), FX ∩ NY = FY . (2.4) Moreover mX < mY , and the strip supports give a canonical X-equivariant surjection σY X : IY −→ IX. (2.5) For three comparable labelled vertices of the same simple type these maps compose: σZX = σY XσZY .

candidates.label: Proposition 2.7
candidates.name: Strict products and saturation
candidates.heading: Proposition 2.7 (Strict products and saturation).
candidates.statement: Let D ≤ X < Y , where Y is labelled. Suppose that the coordinate projections of B = (X ∩ NY )/FY are proper and nontrivial. If [X, Y ] is fenced, or if X is a coatom of [D, Y ], then X is saturated relative to Y . Once B = PIY is such a product, no proper subdirect subgroup of SY contains B. Every coatom of [X, Y ], and every intersection of these coatoms, is saturated relative to Y . These assertions do not require X to be labelled. For labelled X < Y of different simple types the projection hypothesis holds.

candidates.label: Proposition 2.8
candidates.name: One-coordinate projection
candidates.heading: Proposition 2.8 (One-coordinate projection).
candidates.statement: Let D ≤ X < Y , with Y labelled, and suppose that (X ∩ NY )/FY = PIY X , 1 < PX < TY . Suppose also that X is an intersection of coatoms of [X, Y ]; a coatom itself is allowed. Fix i ∈ IY and let ρ : Yi −→ Aut(TY ) be the action of its factor stabilizer on that coordinate. Identify TY with its inner automorphism group, and put H∗ = ρ(Xi). Then H∗ ∩ TY = PX. (2.6) The saturated overgroups of X form a sublattice of [X, Y ], and Z 7−→ KZ = ρ(Zi) = H∗PZ, (Z ∩ NY )/FY = PIY Z , (2.7) is an isomorphism from that sublattice onto the entire ordinary subgroup interval [H∗, H∗TY ]. Original covering relations between saturated vertices remain covering relations after projection. In particular, a strict change of simple type at a cover yields a maximal subgroup of an almost simple group, supplementing its simple socle.

candidates.label: Proposition 2.9
candidates.name: Active-factor transport
candidates.heading: Proposition 2.9 (Active-factor transport).
candidates.statement: Let D < Z ≤ Y be labelled vertices, and suppose that Z is saturated relative to Y : (Z ∩ NY )/FY = PIY Z . Let KZ be the automorphism group induced by a factor stabilizer in Z on a reference coordinate of SY . There are KZ-normal subgroups QZ ≤ RZ ≤ PZ such that (FZ ∩ NY )/FY = QIY Z , (2.8) (NZ ∩ NY )/FY = RIY Z , (2.9) RZ/QZ ∼ = TaZ Z , mZ = aZmY . (2.10) Here aZ is a positive integer. The section RZ/QZ is a chief factor for the action of KZ on PZ: there is no KZ-normal subgroup strictly between QZ and RZ. Its factors give a Z-equivariant surjection τZY : IZ −→ IY (2.11) whose fibers have size aZ. The stabilizers in D and Z of a coordinate in IY induce the same transitive action on its fiber. In addition, suppose X < Z and the hypotheses of Proposition 2.8 hold for X < Y . Set H∗ = ρ(Xi), KZ = H∗PZ, CZ = coreKZ (H∗). Then the subgroups in (2.8) satisfy QZ = CZ ∩ PZ, KZ = H∗RZ. (2.12) Thus RZCZ/CZ ∼ = RZ/QZ is a transitive minimal normal subgroup in the coset action of KZ/CZ on H∗/CZ. The groups H∗ and KZ induce the same action on its simple factors. No assertion that this is the entire projected socle is required. If aZ = 1, the quotient PZ/RZ is soluble.

candidates.label: Theorem 3.2
candidates.name: Chain rigidity
candidates.heading: Theorem 3.2 (Chain rigidity).
candidates.statement: There is an absolute integer B such that every tested chain of length N ≥ B satisfies Ta ∼ = Tb.

candidates.label: Proposition 3.3
candidates.name: Maximal-subgroup input
candidates.heading: Proposition 3.3 (Maximal-subgroup input).
candidates.statement: The following results are used from the classification and representation theory of finite simple groups. (L1) A maximal subgroup of an almost simple classical group, not containing its socle, is a stabi- lizer in one of Aschbacher’s eight geometric collections, or has an almost simple irreducible component. The geometric collections are subspace or flag stabilizers, direct-sum decomposi- tions, extension-field structures, tensor products, subfield structures, symplectic-type groups, tensor-induced decompositions, and forms. Graph automorphisms may interchange the relevant subspaces or flag members; triality and exceptional graph–field automorphisms occur only in bounded rank. We use [1] and the almost simple formulation and descriptions in [22, Table 1.2.A and Theorem 1.2.1, pp. 3–4], with the geometric descriptions in Chapters 3–5; the connected tensor structures and their finite fixed-point versions are also given in [25, Theorem 2 and Section 4(5)]. (L2) The maximal subgroups of alternating and symmetric groups have the intransitive, imprimitive, affine, diagonal, product-action, or almost simple alternatives of the maximal-subgroup form of the O’Nan–Scott Theorem. The relevant formulation and all the alternatives used here are recorded in the proof of [10, Proposition 3.1]. (L3) For a fixed algebraic type, sufficiently general finite subgroups lie between the derived group and the inner-diagonal group of a finite fixed-point group. The complementary alternative is containment in a proper algebraic subgroup of bounded complexity. The bounded-envelope version permits passage to the reductive simple quotients of that subgroup; see [24, Theorems 0.5 and 12.3]. (L4) A subgroup maximal in a maximal subgroup of an almost simple group has at most five nonabelian chief factors [10, Proposition 8.1]. The number refers to chief factors, not to their simple direct factors. (L5) If [H, A] is a height-two interval and A is alternating or symmetric of degree at least five, it has at most eleven interior vertices [5, Theorem D]. Here the entire interval is required to 14 have height two: H is maximal in every maximal overgroup. This is the hypothesis imposed whenever the result is used. (L6) Cross-characteristic irreducible projective degrees satisfy the Landazuri–Seitz lower bounds [23]. In particular, outside bounded rank, a source of natural dimension n and field parameter q requires degree at least qcn for an absolute c > 0; the applicable classical bounds are recorded in [20, Tables 3–6]. Above an absolute classical rank, every perfect central cover of a finite simple classical group is a central quotient of its usual simply connected fixed-point group, uniformly over all finite fields, including the standard graph twists [36, Theorem 1.1 and p. 528]. The central-cover deduction and preservation of representations are proved in Lemma 5.3. After passing to that cover, defining-characteristic irreducibles have the Steinberg highest-weight and tensor-product parametrization [34, Theorems 1.1 and 1.3], including the twisted fixed-point groups [35, Theorem 43].

candidates.label: Proposition 3.4
candidates.name: Factor actions at a maximal step
candidates.heading: Proposition 3.4 (Factor actions at a maximal step).
candidates.statement: Consider a strict labelled cover and its one-coordinate maximal subgroup M in an almost simple group, as supplied by Proposition 2.8. Mark its active nonabelian chief factor. There are absolute positive integers b0, r0 with the following property. (C1) The action on the simple factors of the marked chief factor is obtained through at most r0 transitive action levels. Each level either has degree at most b0, or is the natural action of Ad or Sd.

candidates.label: Proposition 3.13
candidates.name: Reduction to classical one-factor comparisons
candidates.heading: Proposition 3.13 (Reduction to classical one-factor comparisons).
candidates.statement: If Theorem 3.2 is false, then for every s and R there is a retained chain of at least s vertices, with all its original two-edge shortcuts and normal-group tests, such that: (i) all endpoint types are distinct classical types; their ranks, and the ranks of all shortcut middle types, exceed R; (ii) all endpoint multiplicities are equal. Thus each comparison, projected to one upper active coordinate, has one active simple factor; (iii) the killed kernels of all endpoint and shortcut comparisons are soluble. Every endpoint inner comparison has exactly its one active simple factor as a nonabelian composition factor; (iv) there is a pool of absolutely bounded cardinality containing all nonabelian simple types in every projected active-factor and fiber stabilizer in the fixed H∗, and in their induced images, used in these comparisons. No assertion concerns the entire unprojected original stabilizers. The splitting multiplicities and invariant-block indices have boundedly many possible values; (v) each shortcut is either two strict steps, both with one active simple factor and all other inner composition factors soluble, or a strict split followed downwards by an equal-type merge. The latter is geometric. In geometric steps the inactive dimensions have boundedly many possible values once their simple labels and bounded structural choices are fixed; when all inactive components are soluble these dimensions are absolutely bounded. All bounds described as absolute are uniform over the original groups. This proposition introduces no new lattice tests at the retained bottom.

candidates.label: Proposition 4.1
candidates.name: The maximal-step catalogue
candidates.heading: Proposition 4.1 (The maximal-step catalogue).
candidates.statement: Consider a strict labelled cover and its one- coordinate maximal subgroup M in an almost simple group with socle T, as supplied by Proposition 2.8. Mark its active nonabelian chief factor. The non-geometric irreducible category below means that its simple source acts absolutely irreducibly on the ambient natural module and that the maximal subgroup is outside all geometric collections, in particular the subfield collection. All growing-rank assertions refer to growing source rank. There are absolute constants C, c > 0 with the following properties. (C2) For unbounded-rank classical active types, a geometric defining-characteristic step changes natural dimension by taking a subspace or quotient, a repeated natural module, a tensor product, or restriction of scalars. Subfield steps leave natural dimension unchanged and multiply the field exponent by a prime. An extension-field step, read upwards from the active factor, has nt = bns, ϵsfs = bϵtft, ft = ϵs bϵt fs, (4.1) where b is the prime degree between natural matrix fields. A twisted-tensor step has nt = nb s, fs = bft, (4.2) exactly; here b is prime, after bounded source-rank cases are removed. All other changes of field exponent belong to a fixed finite set of positive rational factors. (C3) If there is one active simple component and the other geometric components are soluble, their natural dimensions are absolutely bounded. The active dimension in a subspace case is 26 comparable with the ambient dimension; a totally singular summand and its dual may represent the same active component twice. A nontrivial parabolic radical in these cases has order between qcnt and qCn2 t . For a fixed ambient group, once the active slot, other component dimensions, and the bounded flag/form choices are fixed, there are boundedly many possible orders of the full inner stabilizer divided by the order of its active simple factor, with multiplicity included. (C4) A symplectic-type step of unbounded active rank is cross-characteristic. Its source is symplectic or orthogonal over a prime field of order r, of natural dimension 2d + O(1), and its target natural dimension is nt = rd. If P = M ∩ T, then cn2 t ≤ |P|/|Ts| ≤ Cn2 t . Its target field exponent is at most |Ts|C. (C5) After the twisted-tensor case in (C2) is separated off, a defining-characteristic almost simple irreducible step has a single nonzero restricted, nonnatural Frobenius digit, up to a common Frobenius twist. This restricted module may have further tensor factors in a very special characteristic. Its dimension is at least cn2 s. Its source and target field exponents differ by a rational factor from a fixed finite set. Natural, dual-natural, and natural-size special-isogeny representations are included among the geometric cases instead. (C6) For a cross-characteristic almost simple step, qcns s ≤ nt ≤ |Ts|C , ft ≤ |Ts|C . The upper degree bound also holds in defining characteristic. candidates.label: Proposition 2.7

manuscripts.title: The critical Liouville quantum sphere and geometric limits of FK maps at q=4

candidates.label: Theorem 1.1
candidates.name: The critical area-marked sphere
candidates.heading: Theorem 1.1 (The critical area-marked sphere).
candidates.statement: As γ ↑ 2, the laws of (Hγ, νγ) converge to a unique nondegenerate probability law Pcrit in H−1 (S2 , ground) × P(S2 ), with the norm topology in the first factor and the weak topology in the second. Let (H, ν) have this law and set h = H + log ground in local conformal coordinates. Then ν = µcrit h , where on compact sets avoiding 0, 1, ∞, µcrit h ( dz) = lim ε↓0 (︁ 2 log(1/ε) − hε(z) )︁ ε2 e2hε(z) d2 z (1.5) locally weakly in probability. This positive measure extends across the three marks without atoms, has full support, and has total mass one. After forgetting the three marks, sampling three new conditionally independent area points and normalizing them to 0, 1, ∞ recovers Pcrit. If f maps the new coordinate to the old one, the field transforms as hnew = hold ◦ f + 2 log |f′ |. With any one fixed deterministic normalization of the Ding–Gwynne critical local metric, the compatible chart metrics define an intrinsic length metric on the sphere punctured at the three marks. Its completion adds exactly those marks and is a finite continuous metric Dh on S2, inducing the usual topology. The area and completed metric are measurable functions of the same field and obey the corresponding charge-2 coordinate rules.

(1.6) Here (H, µcrit h ) ∼ Pcrit, the area topology is weak convergence, the distance-graph topology is the Hausdorff topology just defined, and the loop topology is convergence by ε-matchings. All nesting and multiplicities are retained. In the same joint convergence, max T flag of Xn diamρ ϕn(T) P − − → 0. (1.7) The metric normalization is the one fixed in Theorem 1.1; changing it by a deterministic factor changes an by that factor.

With the deterministic normalization of Theorem 1.2, (V (Mn), andn, ηn) d − − → (S2 , Dh, µcrit h ) in the Gromov–Hausdorff–Prokhorov topology, jointly with the embedded area and loop convergence in that theorem.

candidates.heading: Proposition 2.6 (The prescribed limiting probability law).
candidates.statement: The field-measure laws in the con- tinuum approximation of Theorem 1.1 converge, independently of the sequence γ ↑ 2, in round- background H−1 norm and weak measure topology. In cylinder coordinates their limit is obtained from hC = G⊥ − R0 − 1 2 log L, νC = M0/L, (2.5) 16 by sending the two ends to 0, ∞ and an additional independent area sample to 1, using charge 2. Denote this law by Pcrit. It is invariant under resampling three conditionally independent area marks and normalizing them to 0, 1, ∞.

candidates.label: Proposition 2.9
candidates.name: Derivative normalization and area marking
candidates.heading: Proposition 2.9 (Derivative normalization and area marking).
candidates.statement: For (H, ν) ∼ Pcrit, put h = H + log ground in local conformal coordinates. On ˆ︁ C \ {0, 1, ∞}, its law is locally absolutely continuous modulo constants and ν(dz) = µcrit h (dz) = lim ε↓0 (2 log ε−1 − hε(z))ε2 e2hε(z) d2 z locally weakly in probability. The measure extends with zero atoms at the three marks, is diffuse with full support, has total mass one, and is measurable from h. Its fixed-coordinate covariance and its covariance under re-marking are the charge-two rule. The law Pcrit is nondegenerate.

candidates.label: Proposition 2.14
candidates.name: Fixed conformal covariance
candidates.heading: Proposition 2.14 (Fixed conformal covariance).
candidates.statement: For every fixed conformal coordinate map, the local critical metrics of Lemma 2.10 obey the charge-two coordinate-change rule. Equivalently, the metrics d and ˜︁ d above have the same local lengths and hence the same intrinsic distances on common domains.

candidates.label: Corollary 2.15
candidates.name: Short surrounding detours and random charts
candidates.heading: Corollary 2.15 (Short surrounding detours and random charts).
candidates.statement: Almost surely, every regular point has arbitrarily small surrounding rectifiable loops whose metric lengths tend to zero. The conformal covariance of Proposition 2.14 also holds on common nonsingular regions for the random maps obtained from finitely many area samples in the preceding construction.

candidates.label: Proposition 2.16
candidates.name: The metric sphere
candidates.heading: Proposition 2.16 (The metric sphere).
candidates.statement: The intrinsic critical metric on ˆ︁ C \ {0, 1, ∞} for Pcrit completes to a finite continuous metric Dh on the sphere. Its completion adds exactly the three marked points and induces the usual sphere topology. The extended metric is measurable from the original field alone and obeys the charge-two coordinate rule, including the re-marking operation.

candidates.label: Proposition 3.1
candidates.name: Partition function and loop-counting intensity
candidates.heading: Proposition 3.1 (Partition function and loop-counting intensity).
candidates.statement: For a loop let k, l be the numbers of its visited Tutte triangles with blue, respectively red base. Call the side adjacent to the blue bases (i.e. toward the blue endpoints of crossed links) its blue side, and let u be the mn-area of that side of the loop on the sphere, including everything nested there. Write ds(v) = s2v−2 exp(−s2/v) for 27 s, v > 0, extended by zero at v = 0. Then X2n Zn(4) ∼ 8π2 n2 log2 n , lim n E ∑︂ loops ψ(k/Bn, u) = 1 2π2 ∫︂ ∞ 0 ∫︂ 1 0 ψ(s, v) ds dv s5 ds(v)ds(1 − v). (3.1) Here ψ is continuous with compact support in (0, ∞) × [0, 1], extended by zero at length zero. This does not assert that loop lengths can be read from a geometric limit or that every macroscopic loop has k in a range of order Bn.

candidates.label: Proposition 4.6
candidates.name: Marked disk factorization
candidates.heading: Proposition 4.6 (Marked disk factorization).
candidates.statement: For almost every prescribed positive initial perimeter pair, run the independent symmetric SLE0 κ(κ − 6) branch on the corresponding boundary-marked disk. At a fixed surviving trunk time t, conditional on the signed boundary-length path up to t, the offspring discovered by t are independent once-boundary-marked disks with perimeters equal to their absolute jump sizes. Their mark is the actual attachment or disconnection point. Independently, the remaining surface with its tip and target is a twice-marked disk conditioned on its two arc lengths. The assertion concerns abstract marked surfaces and retains the component laws of the unobserved CLEs.

candidates.label: Proposition 4.10
candidates.name: All-point boundary-chain estimate
candidates.heading: Proposition 4.10 (All-point boundary-chain estimate).
candidates.statement: For a disk g in standard twice-typical strip coordinates with perimeter s, paths in its interior approaching any flat boundary point z and +∞ can be joined, along the direction to the right, at cost bounded (including the above deterministic upper weight) by K s2ξ0/γ (︃ m([z, +∞)) s )︃θ2ξ0/γ , (4.1) where m denotes boundary length on that side. The moment quantifier is as follows: for each M ∈ (0, ∞), choose θ < 1 sufficiently close to 1 and then γM < 2 so that sup γ∈(γM ,2] E[KM ] < ∞. The value γ = 2 denotes the limiting disk law. The choice of θ is allowed to depend on M. More precisely we assert existence of connected chains/paths between arbitrarily small neighborhoods of the two points, simultaneously at every z. The reverse statement toward −∞ also holds, and the chains may approach an end on either side using central Whitney slab paths. No exact internal metric extension to boundary is needed.

candidates.label: Proposition 5.3
candidates.name: Critical cutting and the exact contact rule
candidates.heading: Proposition 5.3 (Critical cutting and the exact contact rule).
candidates.statement: Consider a critical field disk with a boundary-typical source and a target at any prescribed strictly interior relative boundary length. Its independent symmetric bSLE0,0 4 exploration admits a trunk-time parametrization in which the left and right boundary lengths have the law of Lemma 5.1. Conditional on the full length path, the jump interiors are independent critical disks with the corresponding perimeters and pinch marks. At the compact-surviving deterministic times and selected jump stops used below, the remaining disk has the marked disk law conditional on the observed past length data. The trunk is a simple continuous arc, all jump domains are Jordan domains, and two contour occurrences have the same physical image exactly when they satisfy the contact relation of Defini- tion 5.2. In particular no side class links two distinct real trunk times, no class identifies distinct points of one outer or jump circle, and no inserted positive circle visits the original boundary. The full exploration, including its ordered loop tours, is obtained as the limit of the subcritical cuttings on compact surviving pieces, with the terminal remainder shrinking spatially to the target.

candidates.label: Proposition 5.7
candidates.name: One auxiliary field for compatible branches
candidates.heading: Proposition 5.7 (One auxiliary field for compatible branches).
candidates.statement: The critical branches can be realized as full signed-CLE explorations of one constant-boundary Dirichlet GFF J, independent of the Liouville input. Branches with the same source and compatible transmitted targets agree until the targets separate, and continue in the resulting components with the signed exploration Markov law. Negative complementary components have the unchanged constant boundary value; positive loop interiors have the signed increment ±2λ and retain their independent Dirichlet fillings. These statements concern the full exploration, including encountered loops. They allow countably many compatible continuations and preserve the abstract marked-disk factorization stated in Proposition 5.3.

candidates.label: Proposition 5.9
candidates.name: Critical sphere cuts
candidates.heading: Proposition 5.9 (Critical sphere cuts).
candidates.statement: For the unit-area critical sphere of Section 2 with an independent nested CLE4, the counting intensity of a loop, a fair choice of side, its intrinsic perimeter s, and that side’s area v has density 1 2π2 s−5 ds(v)ds(1 − v) ds dv, s > 0, 0 < v < 1. The corresponding actual cut surfaces are the critical disk pair with these areas and perimeter, with independent uniform relative boundary phase and independent nested CLEs in the two interiors. Matching is by the intrinsic boundary-length labels. The identity also holds, after integrating scale, as a measure-class identity for arbitrary total area. No uniqueness theorem for critical conformal welding is required.

candidates.label: Proposition 5.11
candidates.name: Compatible target routes
candidates.heading: Proposition 5.11 (Compatible target routes).
candidates.statement: For any finite compatible family of transmitted or independently sampled interior target labels from a common source, the localized path and offspring comparisons hold jointly, for arbitrary converging positive initial perimeters and splits. The same 73 holds recursively in fresh matched jump disks, with the prescribed pinch source or a single fresh common source; transmitted targets are chosen without inspecting the fresh filling. Countably many such observations are obtained by increasing finite tests. Only compatible routes use common prefixes; independence is asserted for fresh components under the marked conditional laws.

candidates.label: Corollary 5.13
candidates.name: Finitely many labels on a fixed frontier
candidates.heading: Corollary 5.13 (Finitely many labels on a fixed frontier).
candidates.statement: Fix a pre- or post-state v of a critical branch. For every physical point z, the set {(α, h) : α ∈ {L, R}, 0 ≤ h ≤ Zα (v), Bα v (h) = z} is finite. This assertion concerns one fixed frontier. It does not bound the number of historical contour occurrences in a contact class.

candidates.label: Proposition 5.16
candidates.name: Spatial comparison under coupled cutting data
candidates.heading: Proposition 5.16 (Spatial comparison under coupled cutting data).
candidates.statement: Consider a pair joined by a central ring of two positive asymptotically equal rescaled degrees, matching equal relative slots uniformly. Take an actual matched continuum pair, a sphere topologically, with the two closed disks glued by the indicated cyclic length alignment. Use any compatible sphere coordinates, possibly sampled from a continuum conditional law. In each disk take a recursive routing as above with continuous trunks, Jordan jump disks shrinking at accumulating jump times (including at terminal), exact quotient contacts, and mesh tending to zero down the nested tiling. This holds in particular for the fresh-target primary experiment. Suppose the pathwise localized couplings and vertex estimates of the preceding paragraphs hold on this countable recursion including the indicated ring alignment. At a matched child the path(s) there are treated within the child’s own chart; a continuation toward transmitted targets can use the pinch slot specified by the split. Then one can align the entire flag spheres by orientation-preserving homeomorphisms to the continuum sphere with vanishing flag mesh so that all sites in matched disks project in the limit within their assigned closures, and the contour, tip/frontier and ring observations above compare uniformly as specified. Full macroscopic loop tours converge with multiplicities and no macroscopic extras if these cutting trees carry the stated CLE, including all remaining loops inside children. This assertion does not control either graph distance or actual conformal distance in the lattice maps.

candidates.label: Proposition 5.17
candidates.name: Joint path, volume, and area comparison
candidates.heading: Proposition 5.17 (Joint path, volume, and area comparison).
candidates.statement: At perimeter scale P = Bn, normalize triangle counts by 2n. In the unconditioned pair construction, all matched cell volumes converge jointly with the compatible path data to the areas of the corresponding critical field disks. Under the homeomorphisms of Proposition 5.16, the normalized flag-area measures converge weakly to the quantum area measure.

candidates.label: Proposition 5.18
candidates.name: Transfer to exact total volume
candidates.heading: Proposition 5.18 (Transfer to exact total volume).
candidates.statement: Fix a compact positive window for the rescaled perimeter of a centrally marked loop. The exact fixed-size counting intensity converges to the unit-area critical sphere Palm law of Proposition 5.9, jointly with every finite compatible surviving path test and every finite collection of cell-volume labels. The spatial, area, and full loop-tour comparisons of Propositions 5.16 and 5.17 hold in this conditioned coupling.

candidates.label: Corollary 5.19
candidates.name: The unbiased topological comparison
candidates.heading: Corollary 5.19 (The unbiased topological comparison).
candidates.statement: The ordinary finite FK sphere admits a joint coupling to the prescribed unit-area critical sphere in which orientation-preserving topological placements give weak area convergence, full nested-loop matching with multiplicities, intrinsic loop-length label convergence, and vanishing flag mesh. Three independent flag-area samples converge jointly to three independent quantum-area samples. The conformal identification of these placements with the prescribed uniformizations and the comparison of graph distances are established separately in the following sections.

candidates.label: Proposition 6.1
candidates.name: Whole-plane walls and local determination
candidates.heading: Proposition 6.1 (Whole-plane walls and local determination).
candidates.statement: There are two signed nested wall systems O, E, coupled with J, with the following properties. (i) Each has the marginal law of a whole-plane nested CLE4. Domain means for O are even multiples of λ and its wall levels are odd multiples; E has the shifted parity. (ii) Under counting Palm measure at a loop, its two side disks carry independent Dirichlet fields with constant side data differing by 2λ, modulo the common period. The nesting on either side is the deterministic level-CLE construction of that side field. (iii) Both systems are determined by J. Under conditionally independent resampling outside an open patch with its field fixed, their arc portions within the patch, together with directions and local data, agree almost surely. This statement does not fix the outside grouping of separated arcs. 86 (iv) The two systems do not cross. If a wall has a proper open arc in one side of another wall and touches that wall, its level equals the actual mean on that side in a common real lift. For two conditionally independent copies of the same system given J, unequal loops cannot meet. All assertions about conditional resampling hold simultaneously for countably many sampled conditional extensions and countably many buffered observations.

candidates.label: Proposition 6.7
candidates.name: Returns and finite capture
candidates.heading: Proposition 6.7 (Returns and finite capture).
candidates.statement: For each return C′ born in a paired sweep of C, C′ ⊂ C. (6.1) Every return is captured as one untouched negative pocket by finitely many ordinary full-fan branches from ∂C, and has empty inherited open target interval. Conversely a complete negative birth with empty inherited target interval is a stabilized return. As the finite target lists increase densely, the two-layer walls stabilize exactly on interior compact sets and the uncaptured negative pockets have uniformly vanishing closure diameters.

candidates.label: Proposition 6.11
candidates.name: Finitely many local callers
candidates.heading: Proposition 6.11 (Finitely many local callers).
candidates.statement: After further buffering, the following data have only finitely many joint possibilities over the compared conditional extensions: canonical callers that have boundary, trunk, or hit-wall operations near K and interact with the exterior buffer; their local open domains and Jordan boundary arcs; their first two half-layer pieces and relevant child groupings; and their half-layer depths relative to the corresponding local shield. A separate common shift is suppressed for each local depth array. Whole internal subtrees have common determined geometry. The finiteness is pathwise, with a random finite cover and random finite lists; it is not a deterministic bound and does not bound the number of preceding remote-only steps.

candidates.label: Proposition 6.13
candidates.name: Local path uniqueness
candidates.heading: Proposition 6.13 (Local path uniqueness).
candidates.statement: Compare ordinary fan paths in locally identical caller geometry, with the same real field J −c. Consider portions from a common directed interior marker 102 to a common later marker B, lying entirely, with room, in the agreement region. Either endpoint may instead be the shared actual source or shared actual local target. In the initial-marker case retain one binary tag: the true-boundary direction toward the target at the first boundary contact in the portion, if there is one. With matching tags the portions coincide. For a common terminal target y this tag is already determined by the boundary grouping and linear order away from the source x: at a contact proceed toward y without passing back across x. The assertion holds simultaneously for the countably many marginal samples and ordinary endpoint tests used above. It requires no new tag at each later boundary contact.

candidates.label: Proposition 6.14
candidates.name: Simultaneous target order
candidates.heading: Proposition 6.14 (Simultaneous target order).
candidates.statement: Use the finite caller patterns and coupled pools above. On a buffered compact observation region, the full family of local target-path portions has only finitely many joint possibilities, including their path order and shared-prefix tree, simultaneously for a dense family of ordinary targets and for length-almost every target. Matching portions coincide exactly. No separate finite choice is introduced for each target. The conclusion holds jointly in a finite cover of comparison charts and is unchanged by increasing or reordering the dense target lists used to represent the fan.

candidates.label: Corollary 6.15
candidates.name: Births and length readouts in matched blocks
candidates.heading: Corollary 6.15 (Births and length readouts in matched blocks).
candidates.statement: The finite local comparison may include positive-loop discoveries, negative cut domains, the positions at which internal children attach to the traversal tree, and inherited target intervals. For a block retained wholly in the agreement region, it also includes its macroscopic length path, elapsed Cauchy clock, and uncharted future tree with the shared internal sources. It does not determine the absolute offset from a possibly exterior path origin. Under a constant local Weyl length scaling, both these lengths and elapsed Cauchy time scale by the same constant.

candidates.label: Proposition 7.9
candidates.name: Exact local gluing projections
candidates.heading: Proposition 7.9 (Exact local gluing projections).
candidates.statement: Fix a finite mosaic history on a supported valid chart. Along a convergent lattice realization, all sufficiently large approximations have their buffered local readouts determined by the retained raw pieces and finitely many affine integer gluing tests. The tests retain every viable closed macroscopic prefix, including singleton cases. Every binding translation is accounted for by arcs inside the private buffer.

candidates.label: Theorem 7.17
candidates.name: Product kernels given the whole tree
candidates.heading: Theorem 7.17 (Product kernels given the whole tree).
candidates.statement: Consider any compatible joint extraction of countably many local readouts from separated retained blocks. There are reference disintegrations kb, fixed for the countable local types, such that the conditional law of the retained payloads given (T , chart) is ∏︂ b kb(dU∗ b | Sb, Ib, Gb). (7.2) The only conditioning within block b is on Sb, Ib, and its actual projection Gb; unused hypothetical continuations are not conditioned on.

candidates.label: Proposition 7.19
candidates.name: Fixed sphere volume
candidates.heading: Proposition 7.19 (Fixed sphere volume).
candidates.statement: The product rule (7.2), with the same reference versions at matched local inputs, holds given the full unit-area sphere input and chart, including after removing Palm weights. A different fresh nuisance reservoir may be used for each finite-cylinder comparison.

candidates.label: Proposition 7.23
candidates.name: Common finite local chart data
candidates.heading: Proposition 7.23 (Common finite local chart data).
candidates.statement: Fix a compact inner test with a strict field buffer. In the conditional exterior comparison with private source pools, successful mosaics can be chosen so that the retained raw-piece instructions, local open geometry and order, interface parametrizations, actual entry projections, and effective macroscopic gluing shifts range over one finite collection. The collection includes all closed viable matching cases and does not depend on the cost units or the readout extraction. This collection is finite almost surely for the common local data and pools; no deterministic bound on its size is asserted.

candidates.label: Theorem 7.24
candidates.name: One finite alternative for a countable kernel vector
candidates.heading: Theorem 7.24 (One finite alternative for a countable kernel vector).
candidates.statement: Let A be any countable family of common cost extractions and fixed unit conversions. Conditional on the local real fields (including their heights), the local auxiliary field, and the private source pools, the vector of full-input conditional profile laws (Kα)α∈A has finite support. Equivalently, one tag T with finite conditional support almost surely suffices to write every coordinate as Kα = Fα(L, T), where L denotes these common local data. The tag is common to all coordinates; its number of possible values may depend on L.

candidates.label: Corollary 7.25
candidates.name: Uniform fixed-label candidate tests
candidates.heading: Corollary 7.25 (Uniform fixed-label candidate tests).
candidates.statement: In a fixed prototype law, the number of candidate kernel vectors and the reciprocal of their smallest positive conditional mass can be truncated once in probability. Arbitrarily high marginal success at a fixed label therefore gives arbitrarily high success for draws from all candidates, with a loss bound uniform in the label. The conclusion concerns each fixed label; it does not require simultaneous success over infinitely many labels. Across separated patches, independent arrays of candidate draws can include the actual selected draws.

candidates.label: Proposition 8.1
candidates.name: Aligned all-point shells
candidates.heading: Proposition 8.1 (Aligned all-point shells).
candidates.statement: Fix α > 0, the buffered annular geometry above, and a countable common extraction of field and regularized-profile observations with its fixed label conversions. Let Ei be a local success test at label i, with strict band margins, evaluated in the fixed prototype probability law. For sufficiently small q > 0, chosen after these fixed comparisons, the following implication holds. Suppose that for each N in an unbounded set of integers there is GN ⊂ [N, 2N] ∩ Z satisfying |GN | ≥ αN, P(Ei) ≥ 1 − q (i ∈ GN ). Then, as N → ∞ through this set, with probability tending to one every point of any fixed planar compact away from the ends lies, with central-hole clearance, in at least βN successful shell holes along its fine-grid ancestry. Here β > 0 and all the radii are at most e−aN for a fixed a > 0. For each label, disks of any fixed large multiple P0 of these radii can be required to have bounded overlap. 139 For each fixed N only finitely many shells are tested, although the number of spatial size levels may be exponential in N. The discrete index is sent to infinity for this finite family before N is increased. The same conclusion applies along jointly extracted subsequences; the required prototype probability is chosen after the geometry, fraction, density comparisons, and simultaneous-candidate requirements have been fixed.

candidates.label: Proposition 8.3
candidates.heading: Proposition 8.3.
candidates.statement: For all sufficiently small fixed ϵ > 0, the quantiles defined in Section 8.3 satisfy lim inf j→∞ bj(ϵ) > 0. (8.1)

candidates.label: Corollary 8.4
candidates.name: Raw extremal-length budgets
candidates.heading: Corollary 8.4 (Raw extremal-length budgets).
candidates.statement: In every diverging perimeter extraction, the following conclusions hold along the good spatial-comparison subsequences. 1. The family of all curves making a fixed positive spherical advance has extremal length bounded below by a strictly positive constant, eventually along the extraction. 2. For circular rings in an ordinary planar chart, with a fixed comparable-radius ratio and fixed comparable buffer margins, there is a strictly positive lower bound on through extremal length that is uniform in radius and location. For each fixed ring test the bound holds eventually along the extraction; the eventual discrete index may depend on the ring.

The actual orientation-preserving uniformizations of the flag surfaces, normalized at these samples, converge along every good extracted subsequence to the prescribed conformal normal- ization of the continuum sphere. The area, full nested-loop, and maximal flag-mesh comparisons therefore hold in these actual uniformization coordinates, in their common joint law.

candidates.heading: Proposition 8.7 (Removal of the auxiliary sampling choices).
